title: RCC RefCert: A Research Toolkit for Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity
description:
RCC RefCert is an open-source toolkit for studying quantum circuit complexity. Given the parameters of your preparation model, you can compute a rigorous lower bound on optimal quantum circuit complexity from final-state data. Use the target state's exact spectrum or counts collected under a prespecified measurement protocol.

The toolkit is based on Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC), introduced by Liu, Tian and Wu in Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity: An Auditable Information-Theoretic Lower Bound.

The GitHub repository contains the source code, a quick-start guide, and worked examples.

Model certification and optimality. You can build a preparation model with measurement, feed-forward and reset, then certify its reference upper bound. In an exact diagonal-preserving model, a program that reaches the target within tolerance is provably optimal if its cost matches the lower bound. If its cost is higher, the gap limits how much a better program for the same task could save.

How complexity varies across subsystems and states. Two states with the same global RCC can have different subsystem profiles. Their density matrices show where the profiles differ, for pure and mixed states alike. Full outcome counts from the same projective measurement give confidence intervals for each state's RCC in that classical window and for the difference between their readings.

Hardware counts and measurement planning. A prespecified binary measurement can rule out preparation costs below a chosen threshold without full state tomography. Plan how many shots to take and how many hits you need, then use target and reference counts to certify the bound with known readout errors. Use your own Qiskit counts or check bit order with 1,024 shots from the five-qubit IBM Vigo processor.

Independent verification. Share the inputs and results in a single evidence bundle so a colleague can recompute the analysis.

Features of reference-contingent complexity

Structural fairness makes circuit complexity comparable across physical settings

Quantum circuit complexity is often measured by the minimum number of gates needed to prepare a target state from a fixed initial state. Counting starts once the inputs are ready, so equal gate counts can conceal different physical costs. For example, one device may supply a pure ancillary qubit, while another must first reset a qubit in a mixed state to obtain one.

RCC takes structural fairness as a physical postulate, using the structure reliably supplied by the background as the reference zero point and fixing the available controls and their costs before the target is chosen. It counts only the resources used to generate additional structure and measures them on a common calibrated scale, making quantum circuit complexity comparable across physical settings.

Final-state data give a rigorous lower bound on optimal circuit complexity

With the model, cost rules and required accuracy fixed, optimal quantum circuit complexity is the infimum of the costs of all circuits that successfully prepare the target. Each such circuit must generate the structure the target requires beyond what the reference already supplies.

Evidence of that structure can come from the target state's exact spectrum or from counts showing that a prespecified outcome is more likely in the target than in the reference. Even when the optimum is hard to compute directly, RCC turns this evidence into an auditable lower bound on the cost of every successful preparation, without reconstructing how the state was produced.

New in 0.4.0

Choose a lower bound on preparation cost to test. Given your expected hit rate, the measurement planner tells you how many shots to take and how many hits you need to certify the bound. Supply target counts together with either reference counts or a known reference response. The calculation can account for calibrated false-positive and false-negative rates.

What the measurement reveals. In the simulated six-qubit cluster-state study, the noisy state and the uniform reference have identical computational-basis (Z) populations. Z-only counts give a zero lower bound on preparation cost. With the same total number of shots, two alternating X/Z settings reveal stabilizer correlations. Each certifies at least one atomic slot, and together they certify at least two slots.

Full release notes

Research tasks

  • Certify a preparation model. Check the combined output of the model’s halting programs against its physical reference. You can reuse a verified reference bound for other targets in the same model.
  • Certify a lower bound on optimal circuit complexity. Rule out every program below the certified cost for a chosen target and tolerance. Use an exact spectrum or counts from a prespecified measurement at a stated confidence level.
  • Compare preparation strategies. Find which programs reach your target within tolerance and how much each costs. In an exact diagonal-preserving model, a successful program that meets the lower bound is optimal. If a gap remains, a better program could save at most that amount. The cooling study finds a six-slot optimum for the full three-qubit target at trace-distance tolerance 1/50.
  • Measure pure-state complexity with window RCC. Subsystem profiles can distinguish pure states with the same global RCC reading. For pure or mixed states, use a density matrix to separate local structure from correlations. With complete histograms from the same projective measurement, bound the difference between two states’ RCC readings in that classical window.
  • Share a calculation for independent verification. Send the inputs and results in one evidence bundle. A colleague can recompute the result from the saved inputs and compare it with the original.
  • Reproduce the paper’s reference calculations. Run python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check. Three MATCH results confirm agreement with the archived expectations, data and report. The paper-to-code map links each calculation to the corresponding equations.

Run the examples

Install version 0.4.0 with Python 3.10 or newer.

python -m pip install "rcc-refcert==0.4.0"

Read the IBM Vigo counts

python -m rcc_refcert study import-counts --example ibm-vigo

The histogram contains 12 observed bit strings. The most frequent, 00101, occurs in 909 of 1,024 shots. To check the qubit order, count the shots in which each end qubit reads 1. The totals are 41 for Q0 and 1,000 for Q4. For your own run, supply the counts and qubit layout to the same command.

Find and verify the optimal four-qubit reset cost

Run the reset task in a new working directory using Bash, zsh or Windows Command Prompt.

python -m rcc_refcert cost template cyclic-reset > task.json
python -m rcc_refcert cost analyze task.json --bundle task.rccbundle
python -m rcc_refcert bundle verify task.rccbundle

At trace-distance tolerance 1/10, the four-qubit cyclic-reset model gives an exact interval of [5,5] atomic slots. A successful program uses five slots including halt, and the model rules out every shorter program. The last command recomputes the result from the bundle. To try another tolerance, edit epsilon in task.json and give the new bundle a different name.

Interpreting the results

In an exact diagonal-preserving model, a certified lower bound and the cost of any successful program bracket the optimum. For general matrix models, the numerical checks report each candidate’s cost and trace distance from the target.

A window RCC reading describes the state at a fixed reference and control bandwidth. A finite-accuracy lower bound on preparation cost also uses the model parameters and one-shot corrections. The scientific scope explains these quantities and their units.
